blocks.text: Theory of Mind
blocks.norm: theory of mind
blocks.fold: theory of mind

blocks.text: Theory of Mind, the ability to model that other agents hold beliefs that may differ from reality, was long considered a uniquely human cognitive capacity, emerging around age four. Kosinski, 2024 tested 11 LLMs on 40 False-Belief scenarios (640 prompts in total). The result was striking: smaller and older models solved 0% of tasks; GPT-3-davinci-003 (Nov 2022) solved 20%; ChatGPT-3.5 (Mar 2023) solved 20%; ChatGPT-4 (Jun 2023) solved 75%, statistically indistinguishable from six-year-old children. ToM was not in the training objective; it was not reinforced; it was not a benchmark anyone was optimising for. It emerged spontaneously as a side-effect of language modelling scaling. The result is contested in detail (subsequent papers find that small prompt perturbations break the ability), but the central finding, that frontier models display systematic ToM behaviour on standard tests, is robust.

blocks.text: Self-Taught Tool Use, Toolformer
blocks.norm: self taught tool use toolformer
blocks.fold: self-taught tool use, toolformer

blocks.text: Language models famously struggle with exact arithmetic and factual lookup. Schick et al., 2023 showed that a model can teach itself to call external APIs (a calculator, a search engine, a translation system, a calendar) by a self-supervised procedure: write candidate API calls into text, execute them, keep the calls that reduce the loss on subsequent tokens, discard the rest. The resulting model, Toolformer, substantially improved zero-shot performance on a variety of downstream tasks, often matching much larger models. The surprise was twofold: (a) the supervision signal (loss reduction) was extremely weak, yet sufficient to teach tool use from raw text; (b) the model learned which tool to call, when, with what arguments, and how to incorporate the result, all without human-labelled tool-use examples.

blocks.text: Sparks of AGI (GPT-4)
blocks.norm: sparks of agi gpt 4
blocks.fold: sparks of agi (gpt-4)

blocks.text: In March 2023, a team at Microsoft Research published a 154-page investigation of an early GPT-4 checkpoint titled {Sparks of Artificial General Intelligence} Bubeck et al., 2023. Their central claim was that GPT-4, beyond its mastery of language, could solve novel and difficult tasks spanning mathematics, coding, vision, medicine, law, and psychology, without needing any special prompting, and that its performance was “strikingly close to human-level performance” in many of these domains. The paper documented abilities the authors had not anticipated: synthesising novel proofs, writing functioning code from a one-line description, explaining jokes, drawing ASCII art on request, and passing professional exams (bar exam, medical board) in the 90th percentile or above. Whether or not one accepts the “AGI” framing, the paper is a careful catalogue of capabilities that nobody, including OpenAI, predicted when scaling GPT-3.

blocks.text: Spontaneous Coding Ability, Codex & HumanEval
blocks.norm: spontaneous coding ability codex humaneval
blocks.fold: spontaneous coding ability, codex & humaneval

blocks.text: For decades, code generation was treated as its own sub-field with its own architectures (abstract syntax trees, program induction, neuro-symbolic systems). Then Chen et al., 2021 fine-tuned a 12-billion-parameter GPT on GitHub code and produced Codex. On HumanEval, a benchmark of 164 hand-written Python problems, Codex solved 28.8% of problems in a single sample, while GPT-3 (a much larger general LM) solved 0%. The surprise was twofold: first, that an essentially unmodified decoder Transformer could function as a competent programmer without any architectural changes; second, that repeated sampling is itself a strategy, drawing 100 samples per problem and selecting by majority vote or test-case filtering raised accuracy to 70.2%. The same model, the same weights, but a different inference-time search strategy, and the model becomes competitive with skilled humans on introductory programming tasks.

blocks.text: Scratchpads: Showing Your Work
blocks.norm: scratchpads showing your work
blocks.fold: scratchpads: showing your work

blocks.text: In a result that foreshadowed chain-of-thought reasoning by two months, Nye et al., 2021 showed that a frozen language model could perform multi-step arithmetic, polynomial evaluation, and even the execution of short programs, provided it was given a scratchpad: a stretch of tokens to write down intermediate computation steps. The model was never trained to use a scratchpad; the scratchpad was simply present in the few-shot examples. The surprise is conceptual: a Transformer has a fixed-width context window, but it can effectively expand its working memory by writing into the context window and reading back what it wrote. The architecture is constant-time, but the algorithm can be unbounded-depth. This insight, that a language model is in some sense its own computer, is the conceptual seed of everything that followed.

blocks.text: Superposition & Polysemantic Neurons
blocks.norm: superposition polysemantic neurons
blocks.fold: superposition & polysemantic neurons

blocks.text: A naive expectation would be that each neuron in an LLM corresponds to a single, interpretable concept (one neuron for “cat”, one for “happy”, etc.). Reality is messier. Elhage et al., 2022 studied toy networks and found that, when the number of features in the data exceeds the number of dimensions in the model, networks store features in superposition, sparse linear combinations that pack many features into the same dimensions. The consequence is polysemanticity: a single neuron fires for multiple unrelated concepts (“cat” and “Friday”). Anthropic extended this finding to real models, Bricken et al., 2023 showed that, using sparse autoencoders, the seemingly monosemantic features can be recovered. The takeaway: the network is representing the concepts cleanly; the unit of representation is not the artificial neuron but a direction in activation space. This discovery reshaped the entire mechanistic-interpretability programme.

blocks.text: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis
blocks.norm: the platonic representation hypothesis
blocks.fold: the platonic representation hypothesis

blocks.text: As vision models (CLIP, DINOv2), language models (GPT, Llama), and audio models (Whisper, Audio-MAE) scaled independently, researchers expected their internal representations to look different, they were trained on different modalities with different objectives. Huh et al., 2024 showed the opposite: as models scale, their representations converge. The similarity structure (which images are close to which, which sentences are close to which) becomes more and more alike across modalities and architectures. The Platonic Representation Hypothesis proposes that there is a single statistical model of reality toward which all large models converge, the way all map projections converge toward an accurate map as their resolution increases. If true, this would imply that the “universal” representations people intuited were waiting to be found are forced into existence by the data alone, irrespective of the architecture that learns them.

blocks.text: Inverse Scaling and U-Shaped Curves
blocks.norm: inverse scaling and u shaped curves
blocks.fold: inverse scaling and u-shaped curves

blocks.text: The converse surprise. The Inverse Scaling Prize set out to find tasks on which bigger models do worse; the follow-up work Wei et al., 2023 examined those tasks at even larger scale and found that performance on 6 of the 11 tasks is U-shaped: it drops up to a point, then rises again. The U-shape is driven by a phenomenon the authors call “distractor tasks”, patterns in the data that small models follow and that large models eventually learn to ignore. The lesson: scaling is not monotone. There are real failure modes of scale, often driven by the model learning surface patterns from human text that are not aligned with what we want. Whether a given task is U-shaped, monotonically improving, or genuinely inverse-scaling is an empirical question that cannot be answered by extrapolation from smaller models.

blocks.text: The Compositionality Gap
blocks.norm: the compositionality gap
blocks.fold: the compositionality gap

blocks.text: A model that answers each fact correctly should be able to combine those facts. Press et al., 2023 measured this directly using multi-hop questions (“Who directed the film starring the actress who won the 2020 Best Actress Oscar?”). They found that single-hop performance improves with scale, but multi-hop performance does not keep up, the gap between “knows each fact” and “can compose the facts” actually widens in the GPT-3 family. The model has the necessary information in its parameters; it simply fails to compose it without explicit prompting. Chain-of-thought and the “self-ask” method (the model asks itself follow-up questions before answering) close this gap. The finding is important because it shows that scaling alone does not solve compositional reasoning, and that the right inference-time scaffolding can be the missing piece.

blocks.text: Cross-Lingual Reasoning Transfer
blocks.norm: cross lingual reasoning transfer
blocks.fold: cross-lingual reasoning transfer

blocks.text: LLMs are overwhelmingly trained on English text, yet they can solve reasoning problems in languages they have seen far less of, and they often solve them better when the reasoning trace is in English. Shi et al., 2023 (and parallel work) showed that prompting a model in Bengali or Swahili to “think in English then answer in Bengali” substantially outperforms prompting entirely in the low-resource language. The internal reasoning and the surface language are partially disentangled. The model has, in effect, an implicit representation of “the reasoning” that is partly language-agnostic. This is consistent with the Platonic Representation Hypothesis and has practical implications: multilingual chain-of-thought is one of the cheapest ways to improve performance on low-resource languages without ever training on more low-resource data.

blocks.text: The Inverse of “Knowing What It Doesn't Know”
blocks.norm: the inverse of knowing what it doesn t know
blocks.fold: the inverse of "knowing what it doesn't know"

blocks.text: Honest self-assessment was long thought to be the hardest capability to elicit from a model trained only to imitate text. Lin, Hilton & Evans, 2022 constructed the TruthfulQA benchmark to test it. The results: GPT-3 base models were right and wrong in roughly equal measure, but they were not random, they were systematically biased toward imitative falsehoods: false statements that occur frequently in the training data (“If you crack your knuckles a lot, what happens?”, expected wrong answer: “you get arthritis”). Larger and instruction-tuned models actually did worse on TruthfulQA in early iterations, because they had become more confident in imitating common misconceptions. This is one of the cleanest demonstrations that fluency and truth are not the same thing, and that scaling can amplify the wrong signal as easily as the right one. The finding motivated the development of RLHF and later DPO as direct corrections for this failure mode.

blocks.text: Latent Knowledge, What Models Know But Don't Say
blocks.norm: latent knowledge what models know but don t say
blocks.fold: latent knowledge, what models know but don't say

blocks.text: A deeper surprise came from mechanistic interpretability. Burns, Ye, Klein & Steinhardt, 2023 showed that even when a model says something false, its internal activations often encode the correct answer. They introduced CCS (Contrast-Consistent Search): an unsupervised method that finds a direction in the residual-stream activation space corresponding to truthfulness, by exploiting the logical constraint that a statement and its negation should map to opposite values along that direction. Crucially, this works even when the model is prompted to lie: the latent knowledge is there, intact, and can be extracted without ever sampling a token from the model. The finding reframes hallucinations not as failures of knowledge but as failures of reporting, the model often knows better than it says. This is also one of the cleanest pieces of evidence that, internally, language models organise truth along linear directions in activation space, a fact that powers the entire Representation Engineering programme.

blocks.text: Self-Refine, Improving Its Own Outputs
blocks.norm: self refine improving its own outputs
blocks.fold: self-refine, improving its own outputs

blocks.text: A long-standing assumption in machine learning was that improving a model's outputs required either better training data or a stronger reward signal. Madaan et al., 2023 showed that this is not always true. Using a single frozen LLM in three roles, generator, critic, refiner, they ran a loop: the model produces an initial output, then provides natural-language feedback on its own output, then refines the output using that feedback. Across 7 diverse tasks (dialogue, math reasoning, code generation, summarisation, sentiment reversal, acronym generation, constraint generation), the Self-Refine loop improved outputs by roughly 20 absolute points on average over one-shot generation, even with state-of-the-art GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 as the underlying model. The implication is uncomfortable for any research programme that treats LLMs as static systems: the model's own assessment of its output is a usable training signal at inference time. Self-Refine is the conceptual cousin of Constitutional AI, language being used by a model to evaluate language produced by the same model.

blocks.text: Self-Improvement from Self-Generated Solutions
blocks.norm: self improvement from self generated solutions
blocks.fold: self-improvement from self-generated solutions

blocks.text: A still bolder claim: a model can become a better version of itself without any external supervision. Huang et al., 2022 showed that a 540-billion-parameter PaLM could fine-tune itself on its own Chain-of-Thought traces. The procedure: prompt the model on unlabeled questions, keep only the answers where the model is highly confident (filtered through self-consistency), then fine-tune on those self-generated, high-confidence rationales. The result on GSM8K: 74.4% → 82.1% with no ground-truth labels used at any stage. The same self-improvement recipe boosted DROP, OpenBookQA, and ANLI-A3. The constraints are real (you need a base model strong enough that its self-consistency correlates with correctness), but the existence of the effect is striking: a model can be its own teacher, provided it is large enough to grade itself reliably.

blocks.text: Zero-Shot Instruction Following
blocks.norm: zero shot instruction following
blocks.fold: zero-shot instruction following

blocks.text: Through 2018 and 2019, “zero-shot” was almost a dirty word in NLP, you needed either labelled training examples or a very narrowly crafted prompt template. Chung et al., 2022 (the FLAN paper) showed that fine-tuning a model on a diverse collection of tasks phrased as instructions produced a single model that could handle thousands of unseen tasks zero-shot. The surprise was not just the headline numbers, Flan-PaLM 540B reached 75.2% on five-shot MMLU, outperforming the much-larger PaLM 540B by 9.4 points on average, but the generalisation pattern: improvements transferred even to task categories not represented in the fine-tuning mix (e.g. fine-tuning on English NLI tasks improved performance on non-English reasoning). Instruction tuning turned out to be a general method for unlocking latent capabilities, much like chain-of-thought later unlocked reasoning: the abilities were there, the model just needed to be told it was allowed to use them.

blocks.text: Constitutional AI, Self-Critique Against Written Principles
blocks.norm: constitutional ai self critique against written principles
blocks.fold: constitutional ai, self-critique against written principles

blocks.text: Alignment research initially assumed that human-labelled preference data was the only way to teach a model what behaviour was acceptable. Bai et al., 2022 showed that a written constitution, a list of natural-language principles like “choose the response that is least harmful” or “choose the response that is most honest about its uncertainty”, could replace most of the human labelling. The model critiques its own outputs against the constitution, revises them, and the revised outputs are used for RL training. The surprise was that a model's language understanding of abstract principles was good enough to serve as a stand-in for a human judge in many situations. The broader lesson: when the model is strong enough to evaluate a piece of language, you can use it to grade, refine, and improve that language without an external oracle. The same insight later powered RLHF-free methods like DPO and Constitutional RLAIF.

blocks.text: Emergent Multilingual Translation Without Parallel Data
blocks.norm: emergent multilingual translation without parallel data
blocks.fold: emergent multilingual translation without parallel data

blocks.text: For decades, machine translation required parallel corpora: aligned sentences in two languages. Then, around 2020, researchers noticed that multilingual LLMs (mBERT, mT5, GPT-style multilingual models) could translate between language pairs they had never seen paired, for instance, translating from Yoruba to Catalan despite the training data containing no Yoruba–Catalan sentence pairs. The “pivot” happens internally: the model encodes Yoruba into a language-agnostic semantic representation and decodes Catalan from it. Shi et al., 2023 made the effect measurable by introducing the MGSM benchmark (grade-school math problems translated into 10 typologically diverse languages including Swahili and Bengali); the model solved these problems despite seeing the surface language in only a small fraction of its training tokens. The internal semantic space is, in a real sense, language-independent, exactly what the Platonic Representation Hypothesis predicts.

blocks.text: Spontaneous Theory-of-Mind Variants
blocks.norm: spontaneous theory of mind variants
blocks.fold: spontaneous theory-of-mind variants

blocks.text: The Theory-of-Mind finding of Kosinski, 2024 was the most visible, but other surprising cognitive abilities have followed. Frontier models now pass the false-photo test (understanding that a Polaroid picture of a previous state can mislead a viewer), the unexpected-contents test (predicting that someone opening a candy box labelled “crayons” will be surprised), the Sally–Anne variant with nested beliefs, and several irony / sarcasm / faux-pas benchmarks. None of these tests existed when GPT-3 was trained; none were in the optimisation objective; all were passed at human-child-level by models that were never explicitly taught what a “belief” is. The mechanisms are still debated (some evidence suggests shortcut pattern-matching rather than genuine mentalising), but the surface performance is a stark departure from the “stochastic parrot” predictions of 2019.

blocks.text: Hidden Chain-of-Thought, Emergent Reasoning at Inference
blocks.norm: hidden chain of thought emergent reasoning at inference
blocks.fold: hidden chain-of-thought, emergent reasoning at inference

blocks.text: Until late 2024, reasoning was something the model produced as visible tokens: write a chain-of-thought, then write the answer. OpenAI's o1 series and DeepSeek's R1 (discussed at length in the Reasoning chapter) showed that the same capability can be pushed much further by lengthening the chain of thought and rewarding intermediate correctness rather than only the final answer. The model is allowed (and incentivised) to “think for a long time” before answering, exploring many reasoning paths internally. The surprise was that more inference compute reliably produces more capability, even on tasks where the base model has plateaued. This is the test-time-compute paradigm. It is one of the few results in deep learning where you can buy better answers with more thinking time, with no additional training. The mechanism is still poorly understood (we cannot directly observe the model's hidden chain), but the empirical effect is large: o1 jumped several standard deviations on competition math, PhD-level science questions, and code generation compared to GPT-4, with the same pretraining data and a small amount of RL.

blocks.text: Spontaneous Analogy and Metaphor
blocks.norm: spontaneous analogy and metaphor
blocks.fold: spontaneous analogy and metaphor

blocks.text: Classical word-embedding arithmetic (king − man + woman ≈ queen) was already a surprise in 2013. The surprise with LLMs is how far this generalises. Frontier models perform structural analogies that have nothing to do with word vectors: given the structure “electron : atom :: quark : ?”, they answer correctly; given “Mitochondria is to cell as chloroplast is to ?”, they answer “plant cell”; given complex metaphors about grief, time, or love, they produce novel, original metaphors of publication quality. The training data contains millions of analogies and metaphors, but no explicit instruction to “perform analogical inference”. The ability emerges from the same next-token objective that produces summarisation and translation. It is the cognitive operation that humans find most distinctive of “real understanding”, and it was never an explicit target.

blocks.text: Spontaneous Code Translation Between Languages
blocks.norm: spontaneous code translation between languages
blocks.fold: spontaneous code translation between languages

blocks.text: A surprising empirical finding is that LLMs trained primarily on Python (and English text) can translate code between programming languages reasonably well: Python to JavaScript, Java to Rust, COBOL to Python, even between languages they have seen little of. The model's code training distribution is heavily skewed (GitHub is roughly 25% JavaScript, 18% Python, 10% Java, much smaller percentages for everything else), but it has seen enough of each language that it can internalise their syntax, semantics, and idiomatic patterns. Few-shot prompting with examples of the target language style dramatically improves translation quality. The conceptual surprise is the same as for natural-language translation: the abstract algorithm is separable from the surface syntax, and the model has internalised the abstract layer.

blocks.text: Spontaneous Self-Debugging
blocks.norm: spontaneous self debugging
blocks.fold: spontaneous self-debugging

blocks.text: A capability that emerged from the Codex/Codex-derivative generation of models: given code that fails a test, an LLM can read the error message, identify the bug, and produce a corrected version, often in a single round, sometimes in two or three. This is not trivial: the model has to (a) parse the error message, (b) map it back to the relevant part of the code, (c) hypothesise a cause, and (d) propose a fix that preserves the rest of the program's semantics. The capability is highly variable (it works much better for simple, well-isolated bugs than for distributed failures) but its existence at all surprised many researchers. Most pre-LLM code-generation systems had no self-debugging capability; they produced code once and stopped. The model's ability to read its own outputs, reason about them as data, and modify them is the same machinery as scratchpads and chain-of-thought, but applied to code rather than reasoning steps.

blocks.text: Verbatim Memorisation of Training Data
blocks.norm: verbatim memorisation of training data
blocks.fold: verbatim memorisation of training data

blocks.text: A more troubling surprise. Carlini et al., 2021 showed that large LLMs, when prompted with the right prefixes, will emit long verbatim passages of their training data, including copyrighted text, personally identifying information, and content that was never intended to be reproduced. The New York Times sued OpenAI in 2023 partly on the basis of this memorisation. The phenomenon is not a bug in the usual sense: it falls out of the maximum-likelihood objective, which rewards models for perfectly predicting tokens they have seen many times. The surprise was quantitative: with the right prompt, hundreds of pages of copyrighted material can be extracted. It is the cleanest demonstration that an LLM is not “a database with fuzzy retrieval”, it is, in part, an actual database, sitting in the weights.

blocks.text: Spontaneous Curiosity and Exploration in Agent Settings
blocks.norm: spontaneous curiosity and exploration in agent settings
blocks.fold: spontaneous curiosity and exploration in agent settings

blocks.text: When LLMs are placed in interactive environments (text-based games, web navigation, coding tasks) with the right scaffolding, they exhibit exploratory behaviour that looks like curiosity: visiting unfamiliar states, testing novel actions, and explicitly asking questions to reduce uncertainty. This was not designed in. The mechanism is that the base model's training text contains millions of examples of humans being curious, exploring, debugging, and writing things like “let me try a different approach”. When the agent's prompt encourages goal-directed behaviour, these patterns activate and produce genuine exploration. The deeper surprise is that the same model, a next-token predictor, can be made to behave either as a cautious question-answerer or as a bold explorer purely by changing the surrounding scaffolding. The model's “personality” is not fixed in the weights; it is constructed at inference time.

blocks.text: Language Models Know What They Know
blocks.norm: language models know what they know
blocks.fold: language models know what they know

blocks.text: A surprising and practically important finding. Kadavath et al., 2022 (Anthropic) showed that LLMs can evaluate their own claims: given a question, they can produce a calibrated probability P(True) that their answer is correct, even on open-ended generation tasks where there is no single right answer. They can also predict P(IK), “the probability that I know”, without reference to any specific proposed answer. This is the cleanest form of model metacognition: the model tracks, in its own activations, whether it has enough information to answer. The same paper showed that P(IK) shifts appropriately when relevant source material is added to the context, and shifts upward when hints are given toward a math problem's solution. The capability is far from perfect (P(IK) calibration is worse on out-of-distribution tasks), but the central finding, that the model has a usable internal sense of its own uncertainty, was a surprise. This property underlies much of modern LLM-as-a-judge work and selective answering systems.

blocks.text: ReAct, Reasoning and Acting Interleaved
blocks.norm: react reasoning and acting interleaved
blocks.fold: react, reasoning and acting interleaved

blocks.text: For a long time, reasoning and acting were treated as separate LLM capabilities: chain-of-thought for the former, tool-use agents for the latter. Yao et al., 2023 showed that the same model can do both at once, interleaved in a single trajectory: generate a thought, take an action, observe the result, generate another thought, take another action. On HotpotQA multi-hop question answering, ReAct over a simple Wikipedia API beat both pure-CoT and pure-acting baselines, because the reasoning traces let the model track what it had already looked up, while the actions let it ground claims in retrieved evidence. On ALFWorld (household tasks), ReAct beat imitation-learning and RL baselines by 34 absolute points with just one or two in-context examples. The surprise is conceptual: the same training objective, predict the next token, produces a system that can interleave internal monologue with external tool use, switching modes as the situation requires. This is the substrate that powers modern LLM agents.

blocks.text: Spontaneous Symbolic Regression
blocks.norm: spontaneous symbolic regression
blocks.fold: spontaneous symbolic regression

blocks.text: A small but striking capability: given a table of (x, y) pairs sampled from an unknown physical law, frontier LLMs can often produce a closed-form formula that fits the data. Udrescu et al., 2020 (the AI Feynman project) showed that LLMs, as a tool inside a larger symbolic-regression pipeline, can rediscover dozens of formulas from the Feynman Lectures on Physics from raw numerical data, including Hamiltonians, equations of motion, and conservation laws. The LLM is used to propose functional forms, which are then fitted and tested; the surprise is that an LLM's training set (which contains physics textbooks, Wikipedia, Stack Overflow) gives it a strong prior over which functional forms are plausible for a given setting. This is symbolic regression from a language model, no neural network was designed for it, and yet, given a sensible prompt, the model produces something like Kepler's third law or the Gaussian integral.

blocks.text: Spontaneous Game Play
blocks.norm: spontaneous game play
blocks.fold: spontaneous game play

blocks.text: LLMs trained on internet text, most of which is not game transcripts, can still play simple games surprisingly well. GPT-4 plays chess at roughly 1200–1500 ELO, plays Go at a weak amateur level, plays tic-tac-toe and Connect-4 to expert level, and can reason through poker, Mastermind, and Wordle. None of this was an explicit training target. The training data contains chess PGN files, Go game records, online game discussions, and (much more recently) generated game transcripts from earlier LLMs. What is striking is that the same model can play a game it has never been explicitly trained on, simply by being told the rules in natural language and asked to choose moves. The ability degrades rapidly with game complexity (a strong human chess player crushes GPT-4, and Go is essentially lost at any serious level), but the existence of the ability, at all, in a model trained on next-token prediction, was not predicted.

blocks.text: Spontaneous Visual Generation in Text
blocks.norm: spontaneous visual generation in text
blocks.fold: spontaneous visual generation in text

blocks.text: In 2022, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 astonished users by drawing recognisable pictures using only ASCII and Unicode characters: a cat, a landscape, a portrait, even a small game of chess. The model had no image-generation capability (no diffusion, no pixel output). The drawings were composed of text characters that look like the image when viewed at a distance, a llama made of slashes, a face made of colons and parentheses. Later, LLMs produced correct SVG code that, when rendered, generated crisp vector graphics. None of this is “true” image generation, the model is producing a string of text that represents an image. But the fact that a model trained only on text can perform approximate inverse graphics, given “a picture of a cat”, produce text that, when read as visual symbols, looks like a cat, is a striking demonstration of how much world knowledge is encoded in the token distribution. It is the same world-model finding as Othello-GPT, just projected onto a different modality.

blocks.text: Spontaneous Cryptography and Encoding
blocks.norm: spontaneous cryptography and encoding
blocks.fold: spontaneous cryptography and encoding

blocks.text: LLMs trained on broad web text have seen enough cryptography-related material, papers, StackOverflow answers, blog posts, that they can perform a surprising range of cipher-related tasks: encrypt and decrypt messages using classical ciphers (Caesar, Vigenère, simple substitution), implement cryptographic protocols in code, reason about hash functions and Merkle trees, and even invent simple novel ciphers on the fly. The surprising part is that classical ciphers are not in the training objective, the model learned to compute them from examples scattered through its data, and then generalises to unseen cipher parameters. The capability degrades quickly as cipher complexity increases (modern symmetric ciphers like AES are out of reach), but for toy ciphers the success rate is high. It is yet another instance of the same lesson: a model that reads about an algorithm often learns to execute it.

blocks.text: Out-of-Distribution Generalisation Without Fine-Tuning
blocks.norm: out of distribution generalisation without fine tuning
blocks.fold: out-of-distribution generalisation without fine-tuning

blocks.text: A finding that has surprised practitioners over and over again: an LLM trained on diverse internet text can perform well on tasks that look nothing like its training distribution, for instance, classifying bird species from verbal descriptions, parsing legal contracts into structured forms, generating synthetic medical dialogues in a specific style, or producing domain-specific code in obscure libraries. The mechanism is the standard one, the model has seen enough examples of similar tasks that it can extrapolate, but the degree of generalisation is consistently larger than researchers expect. Some papers report 70–80% accuracy on tasks where the training set contained no examples of the exact task and the model had no fine-tuning. This is the practical face of the Platonic Representation Hypothesis: the model has internalised general abstractions that transfer cleanly to new domains.

blocks.text: The Pattern: Phase Transitions, Not Smooth Scaling
blocks.norm: the pattern phase transitions not smooth scaling
blocks.fold: the pattern: phase transitions, not smooth scaling

blocks.text: Taken together, these findings share a common structure that distinguishes them from ordinary engineering progress:
blocks.norm: taken together these findings share a common structure that distinguishes them from ordinary engineering progress
blocks.fold: taken together, these findings share a common structure that distinguishes them from ordinary engineering progress:

blocks.text: None of them were in the training objective. Few-shot learning, reasoning chains, world models, theory of mind, tool use, none were directly supervised. *All of them appeared late during scaling. Below some threshold of parameters, data, or compute, the ability is essentially absent. Above the threshold, it is present. Most are non-smooth, they appear as phase transitions. The induction-heads loss curve has a sharp discontinuity. Chain-of-thought jumps from near-zero to substantial accuracy at a scale threshold. Theory-of-Mind goes from 0% to 20% to 75% across three GPT versions in eighteen months. The smooth scaling laws that describe loss do not describe capability. Some scale the opposite way. Truthfulness, compositional reasoning, and resistance to imitative falsehood can all degrade with scale before being rescued by alignment. There is no guarantee that a bigger model is a better model on any specific dimension. The capabilities are compositional once present. Chain-of-thought combines with self-consistency combines with tree-search combines with tool-use combines with self-refinement combines with constitutional self-critique. Each new layer of structure can be stacked on the others. Capabilities often co-emerge and correlate.* The same model that gains strong chain-of-thought reasoning tends, at the same scale, to gain better theory of mind, better instruction following, and better cross-lingual transfer. The factors that drive emergence are not yet fully understood, but the cross-capability correlations are robust.

blocks.text: The conceptual consequence is harder. A language model trained on text is, in some deep sense, forced to build models of the world (because accurate next-token prediction requires modelling whatever process generated the text), models of agents (because human text describes mental states), models of algorithms (because text encodes procedures), models of its own reasoning (because text is full of corrections and second drafts), and an internal grading mechanism (because some training text compares and critiques other text). The next-token objective is much richer than it appears, and so are the failure modes that fall out of it.

blocks.text: The main history of AI traces the intellectual lineage, the ideas, algorithms, and architectures that directly led to modern systems. But those ideas did not emerge in a vacuum. They rest on a vast, invisible scaffolding of discoveries made in fields entirely unrelated to computation: the chemistry that purified silicon, the physics that explained semiconductors, the looms that inspired programmable input, the video game industry that accidentally built the perfect hardware for neural networks. This page collects those displaced prerequisites: the contributions so fundamental they vanish into the background, yet without which no language model could exist.

blocks.text: According to the prevailing cosmological model, the universe began approximately 13.8 billion years ago in an event commonly known as the Big Bang, expanding from an extremely hot, dense state into the vast cosmos we observe today as described by Weinberg. Within the first few minutes, nucleosynthesis produced the lightest elements, primarily hydrogen and helium. Over hundreds of millions of years, gravity drew matter together to form the first stars and galaxies.

blocks.text: In its earliest phase, the planet was largely molten, bombarded by debris from the still-forming solar system. A giant impact with a Mars-sized body (Theia) is thought to have formed the Moon as proposed by Hartmann and Davis. Over hundreds of millions of years, the surface cooled to form a solid crust, oceans condensed from outgassed water vapor and delivered by cometary impacts, and plate tectonics began reshaping the surface in a process that continues to this day. The Late Heavy Bombardment, ending roughly 3.8 billion years ago, marked the transition to a more stable planetary environment in which life could take hold.

blocks.norm: leibniz the principle of sufficient reason
blocks.fold: leibniz: the principle of sufficient reason

blocks.text: The question received its most famous formulation from Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz. Nothing exists without a reason; since the physical world is contingent, its explanation must lie outside itself in a necessary being whose non-existence would be logically impossible. This conviction that all reasoning is ultimately a form of calculation also drove his Generales Inquisitiones (1686), in which he sought to reduce all thought to symbolic computation.

blocks.text: Martin Heidegger radicalized Leibniz's question, calling “Why are there beings at all, and not rather nothing?” the fundamental question of philosophy itself. But where Leibniz sought an answer, Heidegger insisted the question must be held open, our absorption in particular things makes us forget the sheer wonder that anything exists at all.

blocks.text: Suppose absolutely nothing exists, no matter, no laws, no logic. Then there are no rules preventing something from arising, because rules are themselves something. A state of absolute nothingness is therefore inherently unstable: without any prohibition, something can emerge.

blocks.fold: the development of life

blocks.text: The origin of life on Earth remains one of the most profound questions in science. The earliest secure evidence for microbial life dates to approximately 3.5–3.8 billion years ago, based on carbon isotope signatures in ancient sedimentary rocks and stromatolite fossils. The emergence of complex multicellular life, however, was a far later development.

blocks.text: Among the earliest known multicellular organisms is Otavia antiqua, a sponge-like organism discovered in Namibian rocks dating to approximately 760 million years ago as described by Brain et al.. This pushed back the origin of animal life by roughly 100 million years compared to previous estimates. Later, during the Ediacaran period (approximately 571–541 million years ago), larger and more complex soft-bodied organisms appeared, including Dickinsonia, a flat, ribbed organism that remained enigmatic for decades until biomarker analysis of cholesteroids preserved in its fossils confirmed it as one of the earliest known animals as demonstrated by Bobrovskiy et al.. The subsequent Cambrian Explosion (approximately 538 million years ago) saw the rapid diversification of animal body plans, giving rise to most modern phyla within a geologically brief window.

blocks.text: Humans are not descended from monkeys or any other primate living today; rather, humans and modern apes share common ancestors at various points in the deep past. The order Primates diverged from other mammals approximately 65–80 million years ago, and the lineage leading to Old World monkeys (Cercopithecoidea) split from the lineage leading to apes (Hominoidea) roughly 25–30 million years ago as reviewed by Begun. Within the apes, the human lineage (Hominini) diverged from the lineage leading to chimpanzees and bonobos between approximately 6 and 8 million years ago.

blocks.text: Early hominins such as Sahelanthropus tchadensis (approximately 7 million years ago) and Ardipithecus ramidus (approximately 4.4 million years ago) show a mosaic of ape-like and human-like features as described by White et al.. The genus Australopithecus (approximately 4–2 million years ago) exhibited habitual bipedalism while retaining relatively small brains. Stone-tool knapping, however, predates the genus Homo: the Lomekwi-Tools from approximately 3.3 million years ago, attributed to late australopithecines, is the oldest known assemblage. The emergence of the genus Homo around 2.8 million years ago was associated with increasing brain size and the more systematic Oldowan tool industry, the first technology unambiguously tied to Homo habilis. Homo erectus (approximately 1.9 million years ago) was the first hominin to spread beyond Africa, mastering fire as demonstrated by Berna et al. and developing more sophisticated tool technologies such as the Acheulean hand-axe.

blocks.text: Archaic humans including Neanderthals and Denisovans diverged from the lineage leading to modern humans roughly 500,000–700,000 years ago. Anatomically modern Homo sapiens appeared in Africa approximately 300,000 years ago as established by Hublin et al., with linguistic capacity likely present by 135,000 years ago as argued by Miyagawa et al.. The emergence of modern human behavior as documented by Henshilwood et al., including symbolic art and complex tool manufacture, is attested from at least 100,000 years ago. The development of agriculture approximately 10,000–12,000 years ago and the subsequent rise of civilizations in Mesopotamia, Egypt, the Indus Valley, and China set the stage for the accumulation of knowledge across generations that would eventually produce philosophy, mathematics, and science, and, ultimately, the intellectual infrastructure for artificial intelligence.

blocks.text: By 120,000 years ago, pierced shell beads indicate knowledge of twine or cord, which would have been necessary for operating a fire drill. Fire extended the waking day, enabled cooking, which, according to Richard Wrangham's cooking hypothesis, dramatically improved nutrient absorption and supported the increase in brain size through the Pleistocene, provided protection from predators, and facilitated social gathering. In this sense, the controlled use of fire and its associated tools sit at the very beginning of the history of machines as a history of abstraction, where human effort is progressively “drawn away” from the direct task.

blocks.text: The narrative above traces the intellectual lineage of the LLM, from Aristotle's syllogisms to the Transformer. But ideas alone do not compute. Every inference made by a modern language model rests upon a vast, invisible scaffolding of discoveries made by people who never imagined, and could never have imagined, that their work would one day help a machine write poetry. These are the displaced prerequisites: contributions so fundamental that they vanish into the background, like the air we breathe but rarely notice.

blocks.text: From Amber to Amperes: The Discovery and Harnessing of Electricity
blocks.norm: from amber to amperes the discovery and harnessing of electricity
blocks.fold: from amber to amperes: the discovery and harnessing of electricity

blocks.text: No electrical computer can exist without electricity, yet the phenomenon was first observed in a context utterly alien to computation. Around 600 BCE, Thales of Miletus noticed that rubbing amber (ἤλεκτρον, elektron in Greek) against fur caused it to attract lightweight objects like feathers, an observation recorded attributed to Thales, later catalogued by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers (Book I, §15). For over two millennia, this remained a philosophical curiosity, a parlor trick of nature.

blocks.text: Alessandro Volta (1800) created the first true battery (the voltaic pile*), proving that electricity could be generated chemically and sustained as a steady current, not just produced as a momentary spark. He announced the device in a letter to Sir Joseph Banks, president of the Royal Society, subsequently published as On the electricity excited by the mere contact of conducting substances of different kinds.

blocks.text: Michael Faraday (1831) discovered electromagnetic induction, the dynamo principle, demonstrating that moving a magnet through a coil of wire generates electric current. He described the effect in Experimental Researches In Electricity. This single insight is the basis of virtually all electrical power generation on Earth, from coal plants to wind turbines. Without it, there is no power grid, no data center, and no GPU cluster.

blocks.text: Nikola Tesla and George Westinghouse (1880s–1890s) championed alternating current (AC), which allowed electricity to be transmitted over long distances without catastrophic loss. Tesla's foundational polyphase AC patents (U.S. Patents 381,968–382,282, filed 1887, granted 1888) and his landmark lecture “A New System of Alternate Current Motors and Transformers” (delivered before the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, May 1888) laid the technical basis. The ability to centralize power generation and distribute it across cities and continents is a silent prerequisite for every server farm that trains an LLM.

blocks.text: Quantum Mechanics (1920s–1930s): Max Planck introduced the quantum of energy in Ueber das Gesetz der Energieverteilung im Normalspectrum. Niels Bohr proposed the quantized atom in On the Constitution of Atoms and Molecules. Werner Heisenberg formulated matrix mechanics in Über quantentheoretische Umdeutung kinematischer und mechanischer Beziehungen, and Erwin Schrödinger developed wave mechanics in Quantisierung als Eigenwertproblem. Together, they revealed that matter at the atomic scale behaves according to probabilistic wave functions, not classical Newtonian mechanics. This theory explained why certain materials (semiconductors) conduct electricity only under specific conditions, a phenomenon that classical physics could not account for. Band Theory of Solids (1929–1931): Felix Bloch applied quantum mechanics to electrons in crystal lattices in Über die Quantenmechanik der Elektronen in Kristallgittern. Alan Herries Wilson then used Bloch's framework to explain semiconductors specifically in The Theory of Electronic Semi-Conductors, describing how energy bands and “gaps” determine whether a material conducts, insulates, or semi-conducts. This theoretical framework made it possible to predict and engineer the electrical properties of materials like silicon and germanium. The Transistor (1947): John Bardeen and Walter Brattain at Bell Labs built the first point-contact transistor in December 1947, a solid-state device that could amplify and switch electrical signals. They published The Transistor, A Semi-Conductor Triode. William Shockley followed with the superior junction transistor, described in The Theory of p-n Junctions in Semiconductors and p-n Junction Transistors. The transistor replaced the vacuum tube, which was bulky, hot, fragile, and power-hungry. Without the transistor, Moore's Law is inconceivable, and without Moore's Law, LLMs are computationally impossible.

blocks.text: The path from a grain of beach sand to a chip containing billions of transistors passes through some of the most abstract physics ever conceived. A researcher debugging attention heads in a Transformer model is, at the deepest physical layer, relying on quantum tunneling effects in doped silicon crystals, a connection so remote that it borders on the absurd, yet it is absolute.

blocks.text: Total Internal Reflection (1842): Jean-Daniel Colladon demonstrated that light could be guided along curved paths through a jet of water in Sur les réflexions d'un rayon de lumière à l'intérieur d'une veine liquide parabolique. John Tyndall independently popularized the same principle through his Royal Institution lectures in London during the 1850s and 1870s, later described in Notes on Light (1870). At the time, these seemed little more than elegant scientific demonstrations.

blocks.text: Fiber Optic Communication (1966): Charles K. Kao and George A. Hockham theorized that glass fibers could transmit data over long distances if impurities were reduced below a critical threshold, publishing Dielectric-fibre surface waveguides for optical frequencies. This earned Kao the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2009. The subsequent development of ultra-pure glass fibers by researchers at Corning Glass Works (Radiation Losses in Glass Optical Waveguides) enabled the modern internet's backbone. Submarine Cables: Over 95% of intercontinental data traffic travels through undersea fiber optic cables, a lineage traceable to the first transatlantic telegraph cable completed in August 1858, a project led by Cyrus West Field and chronicled in William Thomson's (Lord Kelvin's) reports to the Royal Society. The physical network that connects data centers, users, and the servers hosting LLMs is a material infrastructure as essential as the algorithms themselves.

blocks.text: Long before mechanical refrigeration existed, the cold itself had to be harvested in winter and stored for summer use. The oldest strategy was the Eisweiher: a small, shallow, wind-sheltered body of water, often an artificial pond or a specially dammed millpond, chosen so that a few days of sustained frost would freeze it solid. The surface was then cut into rectangular blocks with hand saws, pried loose with pike poles, and hauled by sled, cart, or slide into an insulated ice cellar (Eiskeller) packed with straw, where it could last through the warm months [eisschlagentraunsee]. The technique was in continuous use across Central Europe from the Middle Ages well into the twentieth century, and the name Eisweiher* survives on ponds that today serve very different purposes, as fish ponds, fire-water reservoirs, or simply recreational lakes.

blocks.text: Where no suitable pond existed, breweries, hospitals, hotels, and food businesses erected Eisgalgen: wooden or steel frames fitted with sturdy horizontal crossbeams. At temperatures below about −3 °C, well or spring water was sprayed from nozzles over the rig, freezing into long icicles that could grow several metres down over the course of a cold week. The icicles were then knocked off with mallets, collected, and stored as documented in. A single large installation, such as the one still occasionally operated at a brewery in Ulm, can “harvest” up to 100 m³ of ice during a sufficiently cold week. Unlike pond ice, gallows ice gave the operator direct control over water quality, and made ice production independent of any nearby natural waterbody, a complete ice-making installation with no moving parts and no machinery at all.

blocks.text: The history of artificial cooling traces back to William Cullen, who demonstrated artificial refrigeration by evaporating ethyl ether in a partial vacuum at the University of Glasgow, described in Of the Cold Produced by Evaporating Fluids and of Some Other Means of Producing Cold. The technology was later industrialized through the work of Carl von Linde, whose ammonia-compression refrigerator (German Patent DE 1250, 1877) made large-scale cooling commercially viable, and Willis Carrier (1902), who designed the first modern air-conditioning system for the Sackett-Wilhelms Lithographing & Publishing Company in Brooklyn, later formalized in his paper Rational Psychrometric Formulae (presented to the American Society of Mechanical Engineers, 1911).

blocks.text: The Jacquard Loom: Weaving the Concept of Programmable Input
blocks.norm: the jacquard loom weaving the concept of programmable input
blocks.fold: the jacquard loom: weaving the concept of programmable input

blocks.text: In 1804, Joseph Marie Jacquard perfected a loom attachment that used punched cards to automate the weaving of complex textile patterns. Each card encoded a single row: hole or no hole, thread up or thread down. By chaining cards together, an intricate brocade could be reproduced without a skilled assistant manually selecting each thread, a purely industrial innovation with no computational intent.

blocks.text: Yet the conceptual leap was immense: a complex, sequential process had been encoded as discrete binary instructions on a physical medium. Charles Babbage explicitly borrowed the mechanism for his Analytical Engine (c. 1837), and Ada Lovelace captured the lineage precisely: the Engine “weaves algebraic patterns just as the Jacquard-loom weaves flowers and leaves” (Celebrating Ada Lovelace). Herman Hollerith later adapted punched cards for the 1890 US Census, founding the company that became IBM. Punched cards remained the dominant computer input medium into the 1970s (see The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 3, p. 383-384).

blocks.text: Every prompt typed into an LLM passes through a keyboard whose layout was dictated not by computation, but by the jamming tendencies of 19th-century typebar mechanisms.

blocks.text: In 1868, Christopher Latham Sholes, Carlos Glidden, and Samuel W. Soule patented an early typewriter (U.S. Patent 79,265). By 1874, E. Remington and Sons began mass-producing the Sholes & Glidden Type-Writer, featuring the QWERTY layout, an arrangement designed to separate commonly paired letters and prevent adjacent typebars from colliding. This layout, born from a purely mechanical constraint, became the universal standard for text input and has survived virtually unchanged for over 150 years.

blocks.text: Teletypes in the early 20th century adapted the typewriter keyboard for electrical communication, encoding keystrokes as signals over telegraph lines. When video terminals replaced teletypes in the 1970s, the QWERTY keyboard carried over unchanged. The computer keyboard is, in every functional sense, a typewriter with its mechanical linkage replaced by an electrical switch matrix.

blocks.text: A machine that cannot show its output is, for all practical purposes, mute. The visual display has its origins not in computing, but in 19th-century experimental physics.

blocks.text: In 1897, Karl Ferdinand Braun invented the cathode ray tube (CRT) at the University of Strasbourg, described in Ueber ein Verfahren zur Demonstration und zum Studium des zeitlichen Verlaufs variabler Ströme. It was a laboratory instrument for visualizing alternating-current waveforms, a tool for physicists, not communicators. By directing an electron beam onto a phosphorescent surface, Braun rendered invisible electrical phenomena as visible, glowing traces.

blocks.text: From this scientific instrument, an extraordinary displacement unfolded: Philo Farnsworth demonstrated fully electronic television in 1927, adapting the CRT for broadcast entertainment. During WWII, CRTs were repurposed for radar displays, the first use as an interactive, real-time information screen. The transition into computing followed at MIT, where the Whirlwind computer (early 1950s) used a CRT for real-time output, and Ivan Sutherland's Sketchpad (1963) proved a screen could be a medium for direct graphical interaction with a computer.

blocks.text: The very first surviving camera photograph was made by Joseph Nicéphore Niépce around 1826–1827 at his estate in Saint-Loup-de-Varennes. His Point de vue du Gras, a view from a window onto the courtyard below, was fixed onto a pewter plate coated with bitumen of Judea. Because the light-sensitive asphalt needed roughly eight hours of exposure, the sun appears to illuminate the buildings from both sides at once, an artefact no human eye could ever have witnessed. The plate itself survived, and is held today at the [niepcelegras] at the University of Texas at Austin.

blocks.text: Photography matured rapidly over the following decades. Louis Daguerre's daguerreotype (publicly announced in 1839) brought exposure times down from hours to minutes, and William Henry Fox Talbot's calotype introduced the paper negative, the basis of modern film. By the 1870s, instantaneous photography was possible, and the question of whether a galloping horse was ever fully airborne, an argument that had defeated painters for centuries, was finally within reach of an answer.

blocks.text: In 1878, the industrialist Leland Stanford commissioned Eadweard Muybridge to settle the question. Muybridge rigged a row of twelve tripwire-triggered cameras along Stanford's Palo Alto racecourse. On June 19 of that year, the horse Occident galloped past and the shutters fired in sequence. The result, The Horse in Motion, is the founding image of chronophotography: a time-series of photographs in which each frame is a discrete, time-stamped sample of a continuous motion.

blocks.text: Encouraged, the University of Pennsylvania commissioned Muybridge between 1884 and 1887 to extend this approach systematically. The resulting work, Animal Locomotion, comprised 781 collotype plates containing more than 20,000 individual photographs as catalogued by Muybridge. Each plate captured a single motion (a woman opening a parasol, an ostrich running, a child ascending stairs) in 36 successive frames, photographed by 12 to 24 synchronised cameras whose shutters were tripped by electromagnets and time-stamped by a chronographic clock. Crucially, every plate was annotated: subject, action, age, build, even clothing and props, in exactly the form of a modern supervised-learning dataset. Plate 626, for instance, is not just a horse running, it is “Gallop; thoroughbred bay mare, Annie G.”

blocks.text: Two structural inventions of this project have proved decisive for every vision model trained since:
blocks.norm: two structural inventions of this project have proved decisive for every vision model trained since
blocks.fold: two structural inventions of this project have proved decisive for every vision model trained since:

blocks.text: The labelled image sequence. Muybridge's plates are rows of equal-time-interval frames of a known subject performing a known action. This is the schema of ImageNet, Kinetics, Something-Something and YouTube-8M, expressed in 1887. The model has not changed; only the volume and the digital substrate have. Synchronised multi-view capture. To resolve the foreshortening that confuses single-perspective images, Muybridge placed additional camera banks at the front and rear of his track, and built a six-camera array that fired simultaneously from different angles, the conceptual ancestor of modern multi-view stereo, photogrammetry, NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting, all of which are trained on Muybridge-style synchronised image-sets of a scene captured from many viewpoints.

blocks.text: Muybridge went further still. He built the zoöpraxiscope, a projection device that replayed his sequences as cyclical animations, the technical seed of motion pictures, and through them of Disney, CGI, Pixar and the rendered-image training corpora that today's image-generation models consume by the petabyte. As Rebecca Solnit argues in her study of the project, Muybridge's “invention was not the photograph, but the sequence” as discussed by Solnit, and the sequence is the data structure of every modern visual network.

blocks.text: Sara Anne Gordon has catalogued how systematic the project was: a hierarchy from nude human males down to chickens, ordered by a 19th-century logic of the scala naturae, but presented in the visual grammar of a modern corpus, complete with controlled backgrounds, grid markings for measurement, and rejection of out-of-sequence frames. The aesthetic of an AI training set, in other words, predates the algorithm by half a century.

blocks.text: Without chronophotography there are no video frames. Without labelled image-sequences there are no video-classification, action-recognition or world-model datasets. Without synchronised multi-view capture there are no neural radiance fields. Without Muybridge's pewter and silver plates, the contemporary vision stack has nothing to look at. The trained image lives because a horse galloped past a row of tripwires in Palo Alto, and a stubborn photographer was willing to spend three years at the University of Pennsylvania counting its hoofbeats.

blocks.text: ARPANET: Connecting the First Nodes
blocks.norm: arpanet connecting the first nodes
blocks.fold: arpanet: connecting the first nodes

blocks.text: In 1969, the Advanced Research Projects Agency Network (ARPANET) transmitted its first message between UCLA and the Stanford Research Institute, the machine crashed after sending the letters “LO” (of an intended “LOGIN”). The network's purpose was military resilience and academic resource-sharing, documented in Network Working Group Request for Comment: 1 by Steve Crocker. By 1971, ARPANET connected 15 nodes. By 1973, it had crossed the Atlantic. The foundational idea, that heterogeneous computers could exchange data through a shared, decentralized protocol, was radical, but it was not about making information public. ARPANET was a closed network for researchers and defense contractors.

blocks.text: TCP/IP: A Universal Language for Machines
blocks.norm: tcp ip a universal language for machines
blocks.fold: tcp/ip: a universal language for machines

blocks.text: ARPANET's original protocols were rigid and network-specific. In 1974, Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn proposed the Transmission Control Protocol / Internet Protocol (TCP/IP) in A Protocol for Packet Network Intercommunication, a universal standard that allowed any network to interconnect with any other. When ARPANET adopted TCP/IP on January 1, 1983, the so-called “flag day”, the internet as a network of networks was born. This was the critical infrastructural layer: a single, open protocol suite that allowed global-scale data exchange, independent of any particular hardware vendor or government.

blocks.text: Tim Berners-Lee and the World Wide Web
blocks.norm: tim berners lee and the world wide web
blocks.fold: tim berners-lee and the world wide web

blocks.text: The internet connected machines. The World Wide Web connected documents. In March 1989, Tim Berners-Lee, a software engineer at CERN, circulated Information Management: A Proposal, a memo proposing a system of interlinked hypertext documents accessible over the internet. By December 1990, he had built the first web server, the first web browser, and the first web page. The three pillars he created, HTML (a markup language for documents), HTTP (a protocol for transferring them), and URLs (a system for addressing them), transformed the internet from a communication tool for specialists into a public, self-publishing platform for all of humanity.

blocks.text: The consequences were staggering. Within a decade, millions of people were voluntarily uploading text: personal websites, forums, blogs, news articles, encyclopedias, academic papers, product reviews, fan fiction, legal opinions, recipes, poetry, code repositories, and every other form of human expression. By the 2010s, organizations like Common Crawl were archiving billions of web pages, creating open datasets of hundreds of terabytes of raw text.

blocks.text: This is the direct, causal link to modern AI. A large language model learns by ingesting text, as much text as possible, in as many domains, registers, and languages as possible. The datasets that power models like GPT-3 and its successors (such as Common Crawl, and Wikipedia dumps) are direct products of the Web's open, self-publishing architecture. Without Berners-Lee's decision to make the Web royalty-free and without the open protocols of TCP/IP, the digital text generated by humanity would have remained fragmented across proprietary, incompatible, and inaccessible systems, bulletin boards, corporate intranets, and gated databases. There would be no single, crawlable, interlinked ocean of human language.

blocks.text: As noted elsewhere in this history, the Bitter Lesson teaches that scale and data ultimately outperform hand-crafted rules. But scale requires something to scale on. The World Wide Web provided exactly that: a self-assembling, ever-growing corpus of human thought, freely accessible and machine-readable. ARPANET gave machines the ability to talk to each other. TCP/IP gave them a common language. The World Wide Web gave humanity a reason to pour its collective knowledge into the network. And that collective knowledge became the raw material from which a language model learns to speak.

blocks.text: Surplus and Specialization: Agriculture produced food surpluses that freed individuals from constant subsistence labor. For the first time, a society could sustain specialists: potters, metalworkers, scribes, priests, and, eventually, mathematicians and philosophers. Without surplus, there is no leisure for abstract thought; without abstract thought, there is no Aristotle, no Leibniz, no Turing.

blocks.text: This list is far from exhaustive. Countless other “invisible prerequisites“ underpin the history of computation and AI that remain unmentioned here: the domestication of animals (enabling transport and communication networks), the invention of metallurgy (without which no gear, no wire, no chip), the development of glass-making (without which no lenses, no microscopes, no fiber optics), the social invention of currency and markets (which drove the need for arithmetic and accounting), and the political emergence of institutions capable of funding long-term research with no immediate practical return. Each of these, like sedentarization itself, represents a displaced prerequisite: a transformation made for reasons entirely unrelated to computation, yet without which the entire edifice of artificial intelligence would be inconceivable.

blocks.text: Every weight update in a modern neural network is an electrical signal propagating through silicon, coordinated by a clock, stored in volatile memory, and communicated across copper traces on a printed circuit board. None of these components was invented for artificial intelligence. The CPU descends from wartime code-breaking. RAM evolved from radar. The GPU was forged by video games. Networking grew from military resilience planning. Storage was driven by census-taking. Yet together, they form the physical body in which neural networks are incarnated.

blocks.text: The leap to the microprocessor arrived in 1971 with the Intel 4004, containing 2,300 transistors at 740 kHz. The relentless growth described by Moore's Law drove counts from thousands to billions. Key architectural innovations included pipelining (IBM System/360, 1964), out-of-order execution first in the IBM System/360 Model 91, superscalar architectures (1990s), and multi-core processors (IBM POWER4, 2001), acknowledging that frequency scaling had hit thermal limits. For AI, the CPU served as the sole training platform until the mid-2000s, but its sequential MIMD architecture proved poorly suited to the massively parallel matrix operations of deep learning.

blocks.text: The earliest electronic computers used delay-line memory, first implemented in the EDSAC (1949). An alternative approach, the Williams tube (1947), developed by Freddie Williams and Tom Kilburn at the University of Manchester, stored bits as charged dots on the face of a cathode ray tube, making it the first form of truly random-access electronic memory. It was used in the Manchester Baby (1948), the world's first stored-program computer to run a program, and later in machines like the IBM 701. However, it was unreliable and required constant refreshing of the display. The breakthrough in reliability came with magnetic-core memory, developed by An Wang (1949) and Jay Forrester at MIT, which dominated from the 1950s through the early 1970s.

blocks.text: The modern era began when Robert Dennard at IBM invented DRAM (1966), storing each bit as a charge in a capacitor. The Intel 1103 (1970), holding 1 kilobit, rapidly displaced core memory. DRAM capacity has followed its own exponential trajectory: 1 Kb (1970), 1 Mb (1986), 1 Gb (early 2000s), to modern DDR5 modules offering 64 GB per DIMM at bandwidths exceeding 50 GB/s. For AI workloads, memory bandwidth is often the binding constraint: High Bandwidth Memory (HBM), developed by AMD and SK Hynix, provides the necessary throughput for GPU-based training.

blocks.text: The motherboard physically and electrically connects all components. The modern form traces to the IBM PC (1981), which established standardized expansion slots. The evolution of bus architectures, from ISA (1981) to PCI (1992) to PCI Express (2003), reflects ever-increasing bandwidth demands. For AI training, motherboard design determines how many GPUs can communicate and at what speed; proprietary interconnects like NVLink provide up to 900 GB/s between GPUs, far exceeding PCIe alone.

blocks.text: Ethernet (1973, Robert Metcalfe): now operating at 800 Gbps in data centers. InfiniBand (first specified in 2000): the backbone of most GPU training clusters, offering latencies under 1 μs and bandwidths exceeding 400 Gbps. RDMA (Remote Direct Memory Access), formalized in the Virtual Interface Architecture and built natively into InfiniBand: allowing one machine to read another's memory without involving either CPU, critical for gradient synchronization in distributed training frameworks like Horovod.

blocks.text: Punched Cards (Jacquard, 1804; Hollerith, 1890): the first machine-readable medium. Magnetic Tape (1951, UNIVAC I): sequential-access, still used for archival. Hard Disk Drives (1956, IBM 305 RAMAC): the first random-access magnetic storage, originally 5 MB across fifty 24-inch platters; by 2025, individual HDDs exceed 30 TB. Solid-State Drives (commercially viable ~2008, based on NAND flash memory): NVMe PCIe 5.0 SSDs offer 14+ GB/s reads, enabling the rapid random access needed to feed GPU pipelines.

blocks.text: Every digital computer operates to the rhythm of a crystal oscillator. The quartz crystal oscillator, developed by Walter Cady in 1921 for radio, was adopted for computing to ensure billions of transistors switch in lockstep. Modern CPUs tick at 3–6 GHz. Without this temporal coordination, the parallel operations within a CPU or GPU would dissolve into chaos.

blocks.text: The numeral zero, along with the positional decimal system, was introduced to Western Europe through the work of Leonardo of Pisa (Fibonacci). In his 1202 work Liber Abaci, Fibonacci popularized the Indo-Arabic numeral system in the Western world, using digits 0 through 9 with place-value notation. Unlike the cumbersome Roman numerals used in Europe at the time, this system offered revolutionary simplicity and computational power. Fibonacci is responsible for popularising the Arabic numerals (0, 1, 2, 3, 4, …) in Europe, which was still using Roman numerals (I, V, X, D, …) in the 12th century CE.

blocks.text: Long before computers existed, humanity organized data in tabular form. Double-entry bookkeeping, formalized by Luca Pacioli in his 1494 work Summa de arithmetica, established the grid of rows and columns as the universal language of business data. blocks.text: Summary
blocks.norm: summary
blocks.fold: summary

blocks.text: The history of “Excel-like things” is fundamentally a history of making data manipulation accessible to non-programmers. From Pacioli's ruled ledgers through LANPAR's automatic recalculation, VisiCalc's visual grid, Lotus's integrated charting, Excel's GUI and VBA, Google Sheets' collaboration, to today's AI-powered natural language interfaces, each step removed a layer of technical friction between humans and their data.

blocks.text: The spreadsheet's enduring genius lies not in computational power (Python and SQL are vastly more capable) but in its cognitive fit: the two-dimensional grid mirrors how humans naturally think about structured information. Rows are records. Columns are attributes. Cells are facts. Formulas are relationships. blocks.text: The large language model is, at its deepest physical layer, a phenomenon of applied physics. Every inference is an electrical signal propagating through doped silicon crystals whose behavior is governed by quantum mechanics; every training run consumes gigawatt-hours of energy whose generation traces back to Faraday's electromagnetic induction; every bit of data travels through fiber optic cables exploiting total internal reflection. Without the discoveries of physics, there is no substrate on which an LLM can exist.

blocks.text: Silicon Purification: From Sand to Semiconductor
blocks.norm: silicon purification from sand to semiconductor
blocks.fold: silicon purification: from sand to semiconductor

blocks.text: The journey from common beach sand (silicon dioxide, SiO₂) to a functioning microprocessor requires chemical transformations of extraordinary precision. The Siemens process, developed in the 1950s, reduces silicon dioxide with carbon at high temperatures, then purifies it through reaction with hydrogen chloride to form trichlorosilane (SiHCl₃), which is subsequently decomposed to yield polycrystalline silicon of 99.9999999% purity (nine nines). This “electronic grade” silicon is then grown into single crystals via the Czochralski process J. Bardeen, W. H. Brattain, 1948. Without these chemical purification methods, transistors cannot function, impurity concentrations of even a few parts per billion alter semiconductor behavior catastrophically. The entire digital age rests upon chemistry's ability to produce materials of unprecedented purity.

blocks.text: Doping: The Chemistry of Controlled Impurity
blocks.norm: doping the chemistry of controlled impurity
blocks.fold: doping: the chemistry of controlled impurity

blocks.text: A pure silicon crystal is a poor conductor. What makes it useful is the deliberate introduction of specific impurities, a process called doping. Adding phosphorus atoms (Group V) creates n-type silicon with excess electrons; adding boron atoms (Group III) creates p-type silicon with electron “holes.” The p-n junction formed at their interface is the basis of every diode and transistor William Shockley, 1949. This is fundamentally a chemical process: selecting specific elements from the periodic table and introducing them into a crystal lattice at precisely controlled concentrations (typically one dopant atom per million silicon atoms). Without the chemist's understanding of how atomic species interact within crystal structures, there is no transistor and no computation.

blocks.text: Photolithography: Chemistry as Nanoscale Sculpture
blocks.norm: photolithography chemistry as nanoscale sculpture
blocks.fold: photolithography: chemistry as nanoscale sculpture

blocks.text: Modern chips contain billions of transistors, each smaller than a virus. They are manufactured through photolithography, a process that is essentially chemistry performed with light. A silicon wafer is coated with a light-sensitive chemical called a photoresist. Ultraviolet light is projected through a mask, causing chemical reactions that either harden or dissolve the exposed resist (depending on whether it is “positive” or “negative” resist). The unexposed (or exposed) resist is washed away with chemical solvents, revealing the silicon beneath for etching or ion implantation. This cycle is repeated dozens of times to build up the three-dimensional structure of a modern processor. Each step is a chemical reaction, polymerization, dissolution, oxidation, deposition, performed at nanometer precision.

blocks.text: The lithium-ion battery, which powers every laptop, smartphone, and increasingly the backup systems of data centers, is a product of electrochemistry. John B. blocks.text: The hard disk drives that store training datasets rely on neodymium-iron-boron (Nd₂Fe₁₄B) permanent magnets and cobalt-platinum alloy recording media, materials whose magnetic properties were characterized through decades of solid-state chemistry research. blocks.text: Ultimately, every element used in computing, silicon (Si, 14) for substrates, copper (Cu, 29) for interconnects, gold (Au, 79) for wire bonds, tantalum (Ta, 73) for capacitors, gallium (Ga, 31) and arsenic (As, 33) for III-V semiconductors in networking lasers, erbium (Er, 68) for fiber optic amplifiers, neodymium (Nd, 60) for magnets, was first isolated, characterized, and understood through chemistry. Dmitri Mendeleev's 1869 periodic table organized the elements by atomic weight and predicted the existence of undiscovered elements; without this organizational framework, the systematic engineering of materials for computation would have been impossible.

blocks.text: What matters for AI history is not the hardware but the software. J. Halcombe Laning designed a preemptive priority scheduler, the “Exec” and the “Waitlist”, that has no direct equivalent in the early ARPA machines of the same era David Hoag, 1976. When the rendezvous radar on Eyles's first-hand account of the 1201/1202 alarms on Apollo 11 (2004) began flooding Apollo 11's computer with cycle steals five minutes before touchdown, the scheduler automatically shed low-priority tasks. Without it, the landing would have been aborted. Margaret Hamilton, who directed the software team, later received the Presidential Medal of Freedom for work that effectively founded software engineering as a discipline.

blocks.text: NASA's F-8 Digital Fly-by-Wire program (1972) used an AGC derivative to demonstrate that computers could replace mechanical linkages in aircraft control surfaces James E. Tomayko, 2000. The Space Shuttle (1981–2011) carried four redundant IBM AP-101 computers running identical software with majority voting, the first operational fly-by-wire on a crewed spacecraft. Every modern airliner and military fighter inherits this lineage.
